title: Thermal study of air conditioning systems for temporary spent nuclear fuel dry storage facilities
abstract: Dry storage is a key technology of spent nuclear fuel (SNF) management. However, no previous studies have examined the application of air-conditioning (AC) systems to indoor dry storage facilities. This study investigates the cooling strategies to reduce temperatures in an indoor temporary SNF dry storage facility during the decommissioning stage of the Chinshan Nuclear Power Plant in Taiwan. A three-dimensional steady-state CFD model was developed in ANSYS Fluent to analyze the indoor temperature field, airflow characteristics, and heat removal performance. The effects of passive natural convection and active AC systems were investigated. The results show that the passive ventilation design provides only limited heat-removal capability because the indoor airflow is mainly governed by buoyancy-driven natural convection and is considerably constrained by the cask arrangement. Adjusting the number or size of windows can slightly modify the local airflow path, but overall cooling improvement remains limited. Meanwhile, an AC system effectively enhances air exchange and reduces indoor heat accumulation. The results show that installing two AC units is sufficient to reduce temperatures to below 33°C at a height of 2 m. This study provides practical design guidance to improve the thermal safety and working environment in indoor SNF dry storage facilities.

title: Experimental investigation of surface inclination effects on ablation of a solid impacted by a hot liquid jet
abstract: In sodium-cooled fast reactors (SFRs), the potential consequences of a severe accident with core meltdown are now considered during the reactor design phase. Such events lead to the formation of a corium , a radioactive mixture of molten nuclear fuel and structural materials. Two protective devices can be implemented in advanced SFR designs: discharge tubes, used to transfer the corium to the lower part of the reactor vessel to prevent recriticality, and a core catcher, designed to receive the corium to facilitate its long-term cooling. However, with such new mitigation designs, the corium may impinge on the core catcher as a high-temperature liquid jet ( ∼ 3000 K ), which can lead to localized thermal ablation of the core catcher. Some design proposals for the core catcher include angled baffles intended to dissipate the jet’s kinetic energy. The ablation of such inclined surfaces must be understood to ensure the structural integrity of the core catcher during the corium relocation phase. The present study investigates the influence of surface inclination on the ablation dynamics induced by a hot free-surface liquid jet impinging on an inclined solid target. Experiments were conducted using the HAnSoLO facility, in which water and ice serve as simulant materials, with a water jet impinging on a transparent ice block. The experimental conditions cover Reynolds numbers from 3.7 × 1 0 4 to 1.47 × 1 0 5 , Prandtl numbers from 2.5 to 5.4, and surface inclination angles from 0° to 45°. Results show that surface inclination strongly affects the filling of the cavity as well as the flow circulation before the pool regime. A new intermediate regime, absent for horizontal impacts, was identified. The results show that surface inclination is not necessarily beneficial in terms of ablation reduction and that, at the highest Reynolds numbers investigated, inclination can lead to an increase in the ablation velocity. These findings provide a first experimental basis for understanding the influence of surface inclination on jet-induced ablation and for guiding further investigations toward reactor-relevant conditions. Their extension to corium conditions will require a progressive validation approach combining numerical simulations and prototypical experiments.

title: A numerical method for coupling parameterized physics-informed neural networks and FDM for advanced thermal-hydraulic system simulation
abstract: Severe accident analysis with system codes such as MELCOR is indispensable for nuclear safety assessment, yet the cost of repeated simulations constrains parametric studies and uncertainty quantification. Data-driven surrogates accelerate these analyses but require large simulation datasets, whereas physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) require no training data yet must be retrained for every parameter change and lose accuracy over long horizons. This study addresses both limitations with the P2F method — Parameterized PINNs coupled with the finite difference method (FDM) — for MELCOR’s Control Volume Hydrodynamics/Flow Path (CVH/FL) module. A parameterized Node-Assigned PINN (NA-PINN) takes the water-level difference, initial velocity, and time as inputs, learning a solution manifold so that a single trained network serves as a data-free surrogate for the momentum equation at all flow paths. The parameterized NA-PINN is coupled with an FDM solver that advances the mass conservation equation at each time step, conserving mass exactly in the discrete sense while replacing the iterative nonlinear momentum solution with a single forward pass. Because the network is evaluated only within one time step and re-anchored to the FDM-updated state, the long-horizon training limitation is avoided. For a six-tank gravity-driven draining scenario, the water-level mean absolute error was 9 . 3 2 × 1 ⁢ 0 − 5 m and the velocity error 3 . 0 8 × 1 ⁢ 0 − 3 m/s at 𝛥 ⁢ 𝑡 = 1 . 0 s. This accuracy holds for time steps from 0.2 to 1.0 s and five initial conditions without retraining or data. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first data-free parameterized PINN coupled with an FDM solver for thermal-hydraulic system-code modeling.

title: Stochastic uncertainty quantification and model validation for burnup calculations in heat pipe-cooled reactors
abstract: Burnup calculations play a critical role in predicting the neutronic behavior and fuel evolution of nuclear reactors over their operating cycle. However, uncertainties in nuclear data propagated through these calculations can lead to significant deviations in key reactor responses. This challenge is particularly acute for long-lifetime non-refuelable systems, such as heat pipe-cooled reactors (HPRs), where accumulated uncertainties cannot be mitigated via fuel management strategies. Such uncertainties are typically addressed with conservative treatments, which reduce confidence in model predictions and introduce excessive safety margins. In this study, a stochastic uncertainty quantification framework is developed to investigate the propagation of nuclear data uncertainties in HPR burnup calculations. Uncertainty propagation is executed through Monte Carlo-based stochastic depletion simulations. To constrain predictive uncertainty, a model validation approach based on a Copula dependence model is introduced, leveraging measurable isotopic concentrations. Results indicate that the uncertainty in k eff increases progressively along the burnup chain due to cumulative effects. Specifically, fissile isotopes such as U-235 exhibit rising uncertainties with burnup, while plutonium isotopes show distinct neutron capture production mechanisms. Furthermore, power distribution analysis reveals elevated uncertainty levels near the core boundary, attributed to neutron leakage. Incorporation of isotopic concentration constraints reduces the uncertainty in k eff by approximately 30%, offering a robust pathway to reduce unnecessary design margins.

title: SKCSP-YOLOv5: a multi-scale feature enhancement network with attention for bubble detection in gas–liquid two-phase flow
abstract: Accurate bubble detection in rod bundle two-phase flow is essential for nuclear reactor safety, underpinning void fraction estimation and thermal–hydraulic model validation, yet existing YOLO-based detectors struggle to jointly resolve small, densely packed, and deformable bubbles. This paper proposes SKCSP-YOLOv5, which integrates Selective Kernel Cross-Stage-Partial (SKCSP) blocks, a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM), and an additional P6/64 detection head that provides a coarse-scale prediction level for the largest individual bubbles, while retaining the same single-bubble detection target across all four detection heads. Across five independent training seeds, SKCSP-YOLOv5 achieves a mean recall of 86.5% and mAP@0.5 of 91.0%, significantly outperforming parameter-matched YOLOv5m, YOLOv8m, and YOLOv12m baselines (19.6–25.9 M parameters; p < 0.001, Cohen’s d > 6) while requiring 25.4 GFLOPs, roughly a third to a half the computational cost of these baselines. Performance is further characterized by bubble size, local density, and occlusion level, together with counting and sizing error, to assess suitability for quantitative bubble characterization beyond aggregate detection accuracy. These results establish SKCSP-YOLOv5 as an accurate, computationally efficient, and statistically validated foundation for automated bubble characterization in nuclear reactor subchannel flows.

title: A deep learning-based surrogate model for Severe Accidents in nuclear reactors using ASTEC
abstract: Integral codes like the Accident Source Term Evaluation Code (ASTEC) are powerful tools to study the physics of Severe Accidents (SAs) in nuclear reactors. Real time SA simulators can also be helpful in training operators of nuclear plants to react correctly to malfunctions. However, SA simulators can take up to several days per simulation, making their use infeasible for real time applications. In this work we show how to speed up a SA simulator with a fast, Deep Learning based (DL), surrogate model (SM). The SM is built as a combination of a dimensionality reduction stage, via an AutoEncoder, and a time-stepping stage, via a Neural Ordinary Differential Equation. The data on which the SM is trained are obtained from the ASTEC simulator, by sampling a set of operator actions for station blackout (SBO) and loss-of-coolant accidents (LOCA). The objective of the developed SM is to approximate multiple spatio-temporal fields for the thermal-hydraulic physics, core degradation, and fission product release modules in ASTEC's vessel domain. The SM predicts simultaneously around $80$ different physical variables (both scalar and fields), maintaining a stable autoregressive rollout up to $50$ thousand time steps. In addition, the AutoEncoder achieves a dimensionality reduction by a factor of over $300$, which allows the SM to predict up to $40$ hours of simulation in under a minute, both on CPU and GPU. This work is the first study of the capabilities and limits of DL based surrogate modeling in approximating the challenging, highly non-linear physics of ASTEC.

title: Sintering behavior and microstructural evolution of UO2-Gd2O3 fuel processed by spark plasma sintering
abstract: This study systematically examines the sintering behavior of pure UO 2 and UO 2 pellets containing 10 wt% Gd 2 O 3 processed via conventional sintering and Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS). The analysis focuses on densification mechanisms, microstructural evolution, and diffusion-driven features related to local Gd redistribution. The results indicate that, under conventional sintering conditions, the incorporation of Gd 2 O 3 promotes the development of Kirkendall-type porosity due to the disparity in diffusion rates between Gd 3+ and U 4+ cations. This effect leads to increased residual porosity and a consequent reduction in densification of the doped pellets. In contrast, SPS processing yields significantly enhanced densification, with relative densities exceeding 97% of the theoretical density, even in the presence of Gd 2 O 3 . The corresponding microstructures are characterized by a higher degree of compaction and a predominance of fine, isolated pores, indicative of improved sintering efficiency. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping reveals a heterogeneous spatial distribution of gadolinium in samples processed by both routes, reflecting limitations in powder mixing and diffusion homogenization. Although forced powder mixing contributes to improved microstructural uniformity, its effect on densification remains comparatively limited. Overall, the findings highlight the superior capability of SPS to mitigate diffusion-induced porosity and to promote enhanced densification and microstructural refinement in UO 2 -Gd 2 O 3 systems.

title: Coupled neutronics–thermal–thermal expansion analysis of a heat pipe-cooled reactor using the SARAX code
abstract: Heat pipe cooled reactors are perceived as promising for providing power supply in remote grids owing to their compactness and safety properties. In this context, thermal expansion plays an important role in inducing sufficient negative reactivity during operation and accident conditions, and thus must be considered in neutronics analysis of reactors of this type. In this paper, a coupled neutronics–thermal–thermal expansion calculation framework is developed within the core calculation module of the SARAX code for heat pipe reactor analysis, with the Megapower reactor as a case study. The coupled framework consists of three main solvers, as follows. The neutronics solver solves the neutron transport equation on arbitrary triangular prism geometry, providing the neutron flux and power distribution. The thermal solver, which includes heat pipe simulation, solves heat conduction in hexagonal geometry and provides temperature distributions for both hexagonal and triangular prism regions. The thermal expansion solver computes axial and radial expansion ratios, repositions mesh points, and updates the geometry accordingly. The axial expansion is assumed to be uniform within each layer, whereas radial expansion is represented by the non-uniform repositioning of mesh points, with their positions determined using the spring method. The three solvers are coupled through a Picard iteration scheme on a unified mesh system. Based on the coupled solution, the reactivity feedback from the temperature distribution is calculated to be −714 pcm, while that from thermal expansion is −640 pcm, yielding a total negative reactivity of −1354 pcm. The temperature distributions of the fuel and matrix were relatively uniform inside the core region, with only a minor impact on the power distribution. The maximum axial expansion reached 2 cm at the top, assuming the bottom layer remains fixed. The maximum radial shift of position in the fuel region was around 5.3 mm at the corners. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the coupled method in capturing multiphysics feedback effects and thus provide a reliable tool for the neutronics analysis of heat pipe cooled reactors.

title: Enhancing Geiger-Müller Dosimetry Accuracy: Error Source Analysis and Process Improvement Using the 6 M Ishikawa Method
abstract: Accurate dose measurement with Geiger-Müller (GM) dosimeters is essential for radiation protection and research, but these measurements are affected by numerous sources of uncertainty that can reduce the reliability of dose assessments. In this study, an Ishikawa diagram was applied to systematically identify and categorize the root causes of errors in GM dose measurements, addressing the need for a holistic understanding of uncertainty factors. The primary objective was to visually map all potential error sources and develop a quantitative uncertainty budget showing their relative contributions.The methodology involved constructing a cause-and-effect diagram that organized the error sources into six main categories: manpower (operator skills, training, positioning), machine (dead time, energy dependence, nonlinearity at high dose rates, detector aging), method (calibration protocol, background subtraction, correction procedures), material (gas composition, filter interactions, detector construction), mother nature (temperature, pressure, humidity, electromagnetic interference, background radiation), and measurement (counting statistics, scale resolution, field uniformity).An uncertainty budget, based on literature data and constructed in accordance with the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (GUM), indicated a combined expanded uncertainty of approximately 54% at the 95% confidence level (k = 2). The main contributors were uncorrected dead-time losses (about 12.5%) and energy and angular dependence (about 23%). The structured 6 M analysis showed that combining the Ishikawa diagram with a quantitative GUM-compliant uncertainty budget provides both a diagnostic framework for identifying error sources and a prioritized hierarchy of corrective actions.This integration establishes a structured pathway from qualitative root-cause analysis to targeted mitigation strategies, enabling resources to be directed toward factors with the greatest effect on measurement accuracy. The findings emphasize the need for comprehensive uncertainty management in GM dosimetry to support reliable dose assessments, particularly in epidemiological and radiobiological studies where large uncertainties can obscure dose-response relationships.

title: Response-dependent layer ordering in fixed-inventory compact neutron–photon shields: Exhaustive OpenMC benchmarks at 2.45 and 14.1 MeV
abstract: Layer ordering can alter mixed-field shielding because each layer receives a neutron–photon field modified by upstream materials and leaves a different attenuation inventory downstream. This effect was isolated in a vacuum-bounded finite-slab shield containing 5 cm polyethylene, 5 cm borated polyethylene, 5 cm iron, and 10 cm concrete. All 24 permutations of this fixed inventory were evaluated with coupled neutron–photon OpenMC transport for monodirectional point-source neutrons at 2.45 and 14.1 MeV. At 2.45 MeV, neutron and photon detector responses varied by factors of 2.52 and 15.61, respectively; at 14.1 MeV, the factors were 1.94 and 1.79. The nominal neutron minimum changed from C17 (Fe–CONC–PE–BPE) to C23 (CONC–Fe–PE–BPE), while the photon minimum changed from C01 (PE–BPE–Fe–CONC) to C19 (CONC–PE–BPE–Fe). Conservative covariance-free leading tiers overlapped only partially. The Pareto sets shared only C13, C17, and C19 ( J P = 0.273 ). C13 remained the equal-weight minimizer under maximum and min–max normalization at both energies, whereas ratio-to-best normalization selected C01 at 2.45 MeV and C13 at 14.1 MeV. For the 2.45 MeV ICRP-116 analysis, C15 minimized the maximum-normalized equal-weight response in all six irradiation geometries. These results show that layer ordering is a distinct, response-dependent variable within the prescribed benchmarks, not a universal shielding rule.

title: Radon gas increasing trend at Campi Flegrei caldera during 2011-2026
abstract: Campi Flegrei caldera is currently experiencing an ongoing phase of volcanic unrest characterized by increasing seismicity, ground uplift (bradyseism), and enhanced hydrothermal degassing. Continuous monitoring of geochemical parameters is therefore essential for improving the understanding of subsurface processes associated with caldera evolution. In this study, a unique 15-year continuous dataset of soil-gas 222 Rn activity concentrations, acquired by the RaMonA monitoring station between October 2011 and July 2026, was analysed together with local earthquake records and meteorological parameters. The influences of environmental variables on radon activity concentrations were evaluated using Spearman's rank correlation and multiple linear regression. The results indicate that meteorological parameters have only a limited influence on the observed radon variability, with regression models explaining approximately 2.6% of the variance for soil parameters and 1.7% for atmospheric parameters. After accounting for these effects, the radon time series exhibits a persistent long-term increasing trend that temporally coincides with the progressive intensification of local seismicity, particularly during the recent phase of accelerated unrest from 2021 onwards. Although the observed relationship does not imply a direct predictive capability for individual earthquake, it suggests that radon variations respond to the long-term evolution of the hydrothermal and stress conditions within the caldera. The presented 15-year continuous monitoring record, unique in the literature, demonstrates a persistent long-term increase in soil-gas radon activity concentrations accompanying the progressive unrest of the Campi Flegrei caldera, highlighting radon as a valuable complementary geochemical parameter within integrated volcanic surveillance systems.

title: Axial Development of Local Void-Fraction and Fluid-Temperature Distributions in Low-Pressure Subcooled Boiling in a Vertical Internally Heated Annulus
abstract: ABSTRACTS The coupled evolution of interfacial structure and thermal fields in subcooled boiling remains difficult to predict, and reliable model validation requires local measurements of both phase distribution and temperature. In this study, an extended experimental database was established for low-pressure subcooled boiling flow in a vertically oriented internally heated annulus. Water-steam subcooled boiling flow was generated between a 30 mm-inner-diameter outer tube and a 10 mm-diameter heated rod over an effective heating length of 2.0 m. Six test conditions were examined by varying wall heat flux, mass flux, inlet subcooling, and exit pressure over ranges of 198–377 kW/m 2 , 376–680 kg/ m 2 s, 12.3–15.8 K, and 115–202 kPa, respectively. High-speed flow visualization was combined with previously measured local void fraction data obtained by optical fiber probes, together with measurements of radial fluid temperature profiles and heated surface temperatures at multiple axial locations. Based on these measurements, the coupled axial evolution of interfacial structure, fluid temperature distribution, and wall thermal response was systematically characterized under varying operating conditions. The resulting integrated dataset is expected to serve as a valuable benchmark for CFD-grade wall boiling closures and interfacial transport models for low-pressure subcooled boiling flows.

title: Simulations of external flow around twisted elliptical tubes for above unity Prandtl numbers and low to moderate Reynolds numbers
abstract: Twisted elliptical tubes are a proposed heat transfer enhancement (HTE) for use in Molten Salt Reactors (MSRs) due to their enhanced thermal performance compared to plain tubes. The twisting ellipsoid geometry causes the fluid to swirl as it passes over the tubes, enhancing mixing and inducing turbulence at lower Reynolds numbers. This effect increases overall convective heat transfer; however, this is at the cost of increased frictional pressure losses. Previous work by the authors has investigated the dependency of cross-sectional aspect ratio ( A R = 1.1 − 2.1 ) and below-unity Prandtl numbers ( P r = 0.001 − 1 ) for this geometry, and this study aims to extend this work by investigating above-unity Prandtl numbers and varying Reynolds numbers. In this study, the Nek5000 computational fluid dynamics (CFD) code is used to perform Large Eddy Simulations (LES) of external flow around twisted elliptical tube bundles. This study aims to further characterize the heat transfer phenomena seen around twisted elliptical tubes when varying the tube aspect ratio, which is a dependency that has not been historically accounted for. Simulations were performed for three different tube cross-sectional aspect ratios (maximum versus minimum diameter), Reynolds numbers of 2000 and 7000, and Prandtl numbers of 10, 20, and 30.

title: Flow-induced vibration response of fuel rod based on transfer-matrix and modal-superposition methods with large-eddy simulation
abstract: Flow-induced vibration (FIV) of fuel rods in axial coolant flow can drive grid-to-rod fretting and, in severe cases, lead to cladding failure, motivating high-fidelity fluid–structure interaction (FSI) analysis with improved computational efficiency. This study develops a partitioned framework that couples large-eddy simulation (LES) of the axial flow with a transfer-matrix and modal-superposition structural solver, where the fuel rod is modelled as an Euler–Bernoulli beam. The framework is verified on a clamped–clamped rod by comparison with an in-house finite element method (FEM) beam model, the Ansys APDL BEAM4 element, and the SOLID187 solid element. The first three natural frequencies and the root-mean-square (RMS) displacements at L /4, L /2, and 3 L /4 agree to within approximately 1% across all comparisons. The predicted displacement spectra accurately reproduce the first three structural modes and their orbital trajectories. Compared with the in-house FEM, the beam-based TMM structural solver reduces the structural computation time by about a factor of four at comparable accuracy for the present single-rod case, and its advantage is expected to grow for multi-span, grid-supported rod configurations, since the size of the transfer-matrix system is independent of the number of spans and lumped supports. Validation against the axial-flow-induced vibration experiment of Cioncolini et al. yields predictions of the first-mode frequency and RMS free-end displacement within 2.4% and 3% of the measurements, respectively.

title: Bayesian inference for 3D activity reconstruction combining X-ray Computed Tomography and Angular Segmented Gamma Scanning
abstract: This study evaluates a Bayesian variational framework for 3D activity reconstruction in 220-liter radioactive waste drums using Angular Segmented Gamma Scanning (ASGS) and attenuation information derived from X-ray Computed Tomography (CT). Computations are made tractable using stochastic variational inference together with a multi-resolution spatial prior for the inferred activities. A CT-to-LAC model is developed to convert CT-derived gray levels into energy-dependent linear attenuation coefficients, allowing the forward model to be constructed under experimental conditions. Tests were performed using homogeneous and heterogeneous mock-ups, with point and linear sources made of either 241 Am or 152 Eu. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first experimental validation of Bayesian 3D activity reconstruction from coupled ASGS and CT measurements for radiological waste characterization. Results show that the approach recovers spatial activity distributions broadly consistent with known source locations. Regarding total activity, for the multi-line isotope 152 Eu, the true activity is recovered within the posterior distribution and the posterior mean outperforms conventional averaging for this multi-line isotope. Posterior mean relative errors ranged from 0.89% to 8.00% across the homogeneous and heterogeneous mock-ups, compared with errors up to 27.19% for the conventional averaged estimate. Posterior standard deviations on total activity were typically about 4%–6% of the posterior mean, indicating well-constrained estimates. In contrast, for 241 Am, reconstructed from the single 59.54 keV emission line, posterior mean relative errors ranged from 26.27% to 42.29%, reflecting combined single-line non-identifiability and stronger sensitivity to attenuation-model errors at low energy.

title: Unfolding the extraction and coordination behavior of actinides by cyclohexyl phosphonate derivatives
abstract: The effect of branching in the carbon chain of phosphonate-based extractants on the selective extraction of actinides from fission products of spent nuclear fuel has been investigated experimentally and through quantum chemical calculations. Although phosphonate-based extractants have been known for a long time, only a few studies have reported the extraction of actinides using cyclohexyl phosphonates. In this study, two dialkylcyclohexyl phosphonate-based extractants, namely di- iso -butyl-cyclohexyl phosphonate (DiBCyHeP) and di- sec -butyl-cyclohexyl phosphonate (DsBCyHeP), were evaluated for the extraction of actinides. The difference in actinide extraction arising from variations in the alkyl chain substituents of the extractant molecules were further examined using density functional theory (DFT) computations to investigate the electronic structure and complexation behavior of the ligands with actinides such as U(VI) and Pu(IV). The extraction performance of DiBCyHeP and DsBCyHeP for actinides and fission products was compared with that of the commercially used PUREX solvent (1.1 M TBP/ n -DD) under identical conditions. The experimentally measured distribution ratios for actinides showed good agreement with the computed binding affinities of the corresponding metal-ligand complexes.

title: Integrating artificial intelligence into nuclear reactor safety: ML-augmented CFD, AI-enabled PSA, and cybersecurity
abstract: This review provides a structured synthesis of how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping safety-critical analysis in nuclear power plants through three complementary technical domains and cross-cutting enablers. First, we examine machine learning (ML) augmentations to computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and reduced-order thermal–hydraulic models, focusing on boiling and critical heat flux (CHF) closures, interfacial transport, transient emulation, and containment-scale mixing. Particular attention is given to physics-constrained surrogates, verification, validation, and uncertainty quantification (VVUQ), and best-estimate plus uncertainty (BEPU) practices that enable credible acceleration of high-fidelity analyses. Second, we review AI integration within probabilistic safety assessment (PSA), covering Bayesian and hybrid graphical models, dynamic event and fault trees, human reliability analysis enhanced by learning-based support, and digital-twin frameworks that embed online updating of risk metrics. Third, we examine cybersecurity in digital instrumentation and control (I&C) systems, including threat pathways, AI-enabled detection and response, adversarial model robustness, and the coupling of cyber–physical consequences with PSA. These technical strands are complemented by recent developments in uncertainty quantification and resilient AI, together with a dedicated assessment of multi-unit and multi-hazard PSA covering inter-unit and inter-module dependencies, shared structures, systems, components, and recovery resources, multi-unit accident sequences, and single, combined, and cascading external hazards. Across all domains, we consolidate comparative evidence, highlight regulatory and explainability requirements, and identify open challenges linked to data scarcity, plant heterogeneity across small modular reactor (SMR), pressurized water reactor (PWR), and boiling water reactor (BWR) designs, and physics–data integration. The outcome is a consolidated map of methods and datasets, together with a lifecycle governance framework for AI-enabled PSA that links intended use, data and model qualification, PSA integration, configuration control, operational monitoring, requalification, and human oversight to auditable decision gates.

title: Experimental study on flow pattern evolution characteristics of gas-liquid two-phase flow in a 3×3 rod bundle channel
abstract: To address the insufficient understanding of two-phase flow characteristics in the small-scale rod bundle channels, this study takes air-water two-phase flow as the research object and carries out a systematic experimental investigation in a 3×3 rod bundle channel. High-speed imaging is combined with a self-developed dual-fiber optical probe system. Flow pattern evolution, local phase distribution, and the time-domain and frequency-domain characteristics of probe signals are obtained under different operating conditions. Five typical flow patterns are identified from the optical probe signals, including bubbly flow, cap-bubbly flow, cap-turbulent flow, churn flow, and finely dispersed flow. A flow regime map is established using a combined identification criterion. Compared with existing transition criteria for vertical rod bundles, the general sequence of flow-regime evolution is consistent, while noticeable differences are observed in individual transition boundaries. The deviation of the finely dispersed-flow boundary from the existing criterion decreases as the gas superficial velocity increases. These differences are associated with rod-bundle geometry, bubble coalescence and breakup, and local disturbances. The local measurements show a core-peaked radial distribution of void fraction, while the radial profile of mean bubble velocity remains relatively uniform. Frequency-domain analysis of the probe signals reveals distinct spectral characteristics for different flow patterns. Bubbly and finely dispersed flows exhibit broadband spectra, whereas cap-bubbly, cap-turbulent, and churn flows show dominant low-frequency peaks with spatial variations.

title: Temperature-Dependent Corrosion of Structural Alloys for Molten Salt Reactors in NaCl-MgCl2 Molten Salt
abstract: The corrosion behavior of Inconel 600, SS316H, and Hastelloy C276 was investigated in molten NaCl-MgCl 2 eutectic salt by 500 h static immersion tests at 550 °C and 650 °C. Mass change measurements, SEM-EDS, and XRD were combined to relate alloy degradation to surface and subsurface microstructural evolution. At 550 °C, all three alloys showed relatively shallow, surface-confined attack without detectable crystalline corrosion products, indicating dissolution-dominated behavior. At 650 °C, corrosion became strongly alloy-dependent: Inconel 600 developed a continuous MgO-rich surface deposit and limited subsurface damage with net mass gain, SS316H experienced dissolution-dominated attack with deep void formation and no protective deposit, and Hastelloy C276 formed a thick but non-uniform spinel layer coupled with significant internal degradation. These results demonstrate a temperature-driven transition from simple dissolution to mixed dissolution-precipitation and show that nominal Cr content alone is insufficient to predict corrosion resistance in molten chlorides, underscoring the need to consider full alloy chemistry and salt impurity effects in materials selection for chloride-based molten salt systems.

title: Radionuclide production cross-sections from proton-induced reactions on natural iron up to 100 MeV
abstract: The production cross-sections of 55,56,57 Co, 52g Fe, 52g,54 Mn, 48,51 Cr, and 48 V from nat Fe(p,x) reactions were determined at the Korea Multi-purpose Accelerator Complex (KOMAC) for proton energies up to 100 MeV. Stacked-foil irradiations were followed by off-line γ-ray spectrometry using an HPGe detector. The proton beam flux was determined using the 27 Al(p,x) 24 Na monitor reaction. The present data combined with our earlier measurements using a 57 MeV proton beam provide excitation functions covering the energy range from the reaction thresholds up to 100 MeV. The excitation functions obtained in this study are generally consistent with the available experimental data in the literature, whereas the level of agreement with the TENDL-2025 evaluated nuclear data library varies depending on the radionuclide and proton energy region.

title: Waste classification of PWR concrete biological shield: Impact of detector-window cavities on neutron streaming
abstract: Concrete biological shields (CBSs) of large pressurized water reactors (PWRs) yield a significant amount of waste upon decommissioning, and neutron-transport and activation calculations are useful tools for evaluating their radioactivity distributions. However, the impact of the geometric modeling fidelity of the calculation models on decommissioning waste management is not fully understood. This study focused on detector-window (DW) cavities in the CBS and investigated the effects of DW on radioactive waste classification for a representative 4-loop PWR using the three-dimensional continuous-energy Monte Carlo transport simulation code PHITS and its post-processing multi-group activation code DCHAIN-PHITS. The air-filled DW cavity formed a low-attenuation streaming path, producing higher neutron flux near the cavity end and in the deep CBS region. These neutron-flux characteristics were reflected in the spatial distribution of activation products with a bulge around the DW and thus in the waste-class boundaries. Applying Japanese regulatory criteria, the DW cavity produced a bulge in the L3 (VLLW)-clearance boundary in the DW direction, and this effect persisted throughout the cooling time. In contrast, the influence of the DW cavity on the L2 (LLW) region was limited, because the L2 waste diminished as 60 Co decayed. These results demonstrated that the localized deep activation near DW openings is significant enough for considering waste minimization through clearance.

title: Temperature–based quantitative detection of micro–internal leakage in heat–cycle isolation valves of nuclear power plants
abstract: The internal leakage of heat-cycle isolation valves in nuclear power plants impairs plant economics and may trigger environmental contamination or safety issues due to medium release. Non-destructive, on-line and quantitative detection methods are therefore urgently required. Among existing techniques, the temperature method is the most promising for quantitative on-line leakage detection of high-temperature valves; however, the coupled multi-physics nature of micro-leakage and their invisibility make both identification and quantification challenging. Taking actual plant pressure and temperature as boundary conditions, artificial valve defects were designed and a fluid-thermal-solid coupled CFD model was built. Temperature-characteristic parameters extracted from the simulated outer-wall temperature field were correlated with leakage rate by combining the least-squares method with multiple linear regression. Experimental validation showed predicted leakage rates agree with measured values within a mean relative error of 6% and the minimum detectable leakage is 2 L/h, outperforming traditional models. The temperature-based predictor therefore offers practical value for enhanced online monitoring and predictive maintenance in nuclear power plants.

title: NUCLEA: A thermodynamic database validated for severe accident codes
abstract: The objective of this article is to present an overview of the validation of the NUCLEA thermodynamic database through a comparative analysis with experimental data. These examples are selected from important experimental programs (notably OECD MASCA, EC ENTHALPY) in order to cover various important topics for improving severe accident codes, especially regarding the progression of corium inside or outside the vessel. The comparison between calculations and measurements is discussed, and the main lessons learned from this extensive validation work are summarized, along with an assessment of the current relevance of the NUCLEA database concerning the thermodynamics of corium. Based on these results, the validity domain of NUCLEA is defined, and prospects for future improvement are proposed.

title: Molten salt reactors: Design concepts, global development status, and technical challenges
abstract: Molten salt reactors (MSRs) have re-emerged as a promising class of advanced nuclear systems due to their potential for high-temperature operation, low-pressure operation, and flexible fuel-cycle strategies. In contrast to conventional solid-fuel reactors, MSRs employ either circulating liquid fuel or molten-salt coolants, enabling strong coupling among neutronics, thermal-hydraulics, chemistry, and fuel-composition evolution during operation. This review presents a comprehensive overview of the state of the art in MSR technology, with particular emphasis on liquid-fueled systems and thorium-based fuel cycles. It discusses key aspects of MSR development, including historical evolution, reactor classification, core design and neutronics, salt chemistry and materials compatibility, thermal-hydraulics, and multiphysics modeling. In addition, MSR-specific topics such as fuel-cycle and reprocessing strategies, safety behavior, source-term characteristics, and global development activities are examined. Particular attention is given to the interdependence of design choices, highlighting how fuel form, neutron spectrum, salt chemistry, and fuel-cycle strategy collectively influence reactor performance, technical complexity, and deployment feasibility. As a central synthesis, this review identifies a key tradeoff between fuel utilization and system complexity across near-term and long-term MSR concepts. Finally, it concludes that continued MSR progress will depend on integrated demonstrations of reactor physics, chemistry, materials performance, fuel processing, safety behavior, and system-level operation, while also addressing the major technical and regulatory challenges that remain for future advancement.

title: Assessment of a twisted double-tube latent heat storage system from the perspectives of the first and second laws of thermodynamics throughout the melting and solidification processes
abstract: The current study numerically investigates the impact of twist angle on the performance of a twisted double-tube latent heat storage (LHS) system, evaluating first- and second-law efficiencies during melting and solidification. Water serves as the heat transfer fluid (HTF) circulating within the inner tube, while the phase change material (PCM) RT35 is situated in the annular space. Performance is evaluated by examining the PCM temperature, liquid fraction, and the rates of thermal and frictional entropy generation over time. The findings indicate that lower twist angles result in reduced melting and solidification durations. A notable exception is the 360° case during melting, which achieves the shortest melting time among all configurations due to the dominance of vortex-enhanced convective heat transfer over the minor stagnation-zone penalty at this twist angle. Frictional entropy generation is consistently negligible compared to thermal entropy generation. Thermal entropy generation exhibits an increasing-then-decreasing trend during solidification, with peak values of 7.8 W/m 3 /K and 1.8 W/m 3 /K recorded during solidification and melting, respectively. At higher twist angles, both phase-change durations are extended.

title: Updates to Dynamic Functions in the GAMMA-PC Methodology for Dry Storage Loading Optimization
abstract: This article presents updates to the Greedy Adaptive Multi-Objective Memetic Algorithm with Partial Clustering (GAMMA-PC), an evolutionary algorithm designed to select used nuclear fuel assemblies for dry storage over a reactor’s lifetime. The algorithm simultaneously minimizes the number of canisters, the average initial heat load, and the maximum time to transportation readiness. The U.S. Department of Energy developed GAMMA-PC for integration with the STANDARDS used nuclear fuel data and analysis tool. The tool was recently updated to enable user-defined loading schedules. This functionality was tested by comparing GAMMA-PC’s performance using the default continuous timeline versus the new scheduling-friendly timeline.Comanche Peak Nuclear Power Plant was chosen as a test case. For the discrete schedule, five dates were provided from 2019 to 2025 followed by a loading frequency of every 24 months. GAMMA-PC performed as well as or better than status quo (i.e. the default continuous timeline) when using the discrete timeline. A staggered optimization approach was also tested to simulate how a utility might use the software. Each stage of the optimization ran one-fifth of the number of function evaluations, resulting in a solution that was comparable to the single longer run. This suggests that GAMMA-PC might not need as long to converge toward the Pareto front as originally expected. These improvements add a new functionality and demonstrate the continued usefulness of GAMMA-PC in dry storage loading and scheduling optimization.

title: Proposition of New Structures to the “Don’t Know” Classification Applied to the Problem of Diagnostic of Abnormal Situations in Nuclear Power Plants
abstract: Machine learning, a field that has grown in the past years, includes applications in the Nuclear Engineering domain. The problem of diagnostic of abnormal situations (PDAS) can be seen as an application of the separation problem of machine learning to help operators understand the signals in the control room in nuclear power plants. To avoid returning wrong responses that could worsen the judgment of the operator, a methodology called “Don’t know” has been developed and applied to the PDAS problem. This article introduces new geometrical structures with the objective of upgrading the Don’t know model proposed in the literature, improving its accuracy, precision, recall, and specificity using a new proposition of algorithm H-QEA, based on the quantum-inspired evolutionary algorithm, to optimize the classification of events.

title: Digital Twin–Driven Nuclear Power Plant Health Monitoring, Diagnostics, and Prognostics
abstract: Nuclear energy has the potential to significantly change the energy production landscape in the United States, meeting the nation’s energy demands in a sustainable and environmentally responsible manner. However, the economics associated with operating the aging nuclear power plants (NPPs) require improvement while maintaining their high availability. The U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Nuclear Energy has been focusing on key research and development initiatives for the advancement of nuclear energy, such as technologies and solutions to improve reliability, sustain the safety, and extend the life of current reactors.This paper highlights the research to deliver an integrated decision support system for NPPs to provide improvements to the operations and maintenance (O&M) costs across the complete life cycle of a light water reactor, from design and deployment to O&M. The underlying driver of the improved O&M costs is our hybrid approach with a data-driven analysis and model-based systems engineering approach that utilizes a common model for all sustainment phases.The research team devised an approach to map anomalies discovered through data-driven or physics-based models to specific root causes using digital twins. Any previously undiscovered anomaly can be augmented in the system model via a continuous improvement process that allows analysts to view cause-effect relationships for the anomaly within a model-based perspective and helps associate failure causes to the anomaly.The research team derived degradation indicators based on the hybrid approach and applied them to data gathered from the circulating water system of an operating NPP covering a period of 14 years. The indicators performed moderately well owing to the lack of data quality and consistency, with a false positive rate ranging from 0% to 33% and a false negative rate ranging from 11% to 50%. This technology has the potential to reduce O&M costs and increase NPP reliability and lifespan.

title: Design and Optimization of a Low-Background Shielding System for Gaseous Tritium Measurement
abstract: Sensitive measurement of residual tritium in 3 He is important for radiation safety and product quality, but low-energy background limits the measurement of low-activity gaseous tritium. The contribution of multiple environmental and shielding-related background sources is difficult to quantify separately. This study proposes a source-resolved Monte Carlo approach in which the environmental radiation field is constrained by an ambient dose rate of 0.1 μSv/h, and individual background sources are modeled and quantified separately. The resulting source contributions are used to identify the dominant backgrounds and optimize a graded Pb/Cu/PMMA shielding structure. A lead thickness of about 7 cm, together with 1 mm Cu and 3 mm PMMA liners, was selected to suppress the dominant γ-ray and characteristic X-ray backgrounds. The optimized system yielded simulated and experimental background count rates of 0.145 ± 0.003 and 0.183 ± 0.014 cps, respectively, corresponding to MDAs of 0.35 and 0.44 Bq/L (@60min). The results demonstrate that source-resolved background quantification provides a practical basis for shielding optimization and low-background gaseous tritium measurement.

title: Automating real-time recovery from radiation-induced errors with byte-sized corrections
abstract: Radiation-induced errors in high-energy physics detectors threaten data integrity and uptime, posing significant challenges for reliable operation during the future high-luminosity LHC runs. With over 150,000 ASICs to be deployed in the CMS HGCAL front-end, even a very low per-chip error probability results in a non-negligible failure rate. This work presents a firmware-based, byte-level autorecovery mechanism for the CMS HGCAL Phase-2 front-end electronics, capable of detecting transient upset-related errors and restoring chip operation in real time without requiring a full system reset, ensuring data acquisition continues uninterrupted. The system, implemented in FPGA logic and validated using front-end emulation, executes recovery actions within 4.7 µs, corresponding to the measured interval from the data acquisition signal to packet arrival. Overall, the hardware approach is measured to recover approximately 73.5 ms faster than software-based intervention. The results demonstrate robust, autonomous operation in radiation-prone environments while preserving continuous data acquisition.

title: An advanced solution for nuclear safety I&C software: Deep integration of model-driven development and formal methods
abstract: Instrumentation and control (I&C) systems constitute the central nervous system of a nuclear power plant. In digital I&C systems, software is the core carrier of functionality and may be regarded as the “cognition” of the plant. With the rapid growth in both the complexity and scale of software functions, software reliability—especially for safety-class software—has become a critical challenge. Formal methods offer a promising solution to this challenge; however, in the nuclear domain, their application remains fragmented and exploratory, lacking a systematic methodology and integrated framework. In this paper, we propose a deeply integrated framework that combines model-driven development with formal methods across the entire software lifecycle. The framework addresses, in a formal and unified manner: (1) the precision of software requirements and design specifications, (2) behavioral consistency between software design and implementation, and (3) conformance of software design to formalized requirements. The framework integrates formal requirements specification, synchronous dataflow-based design modeling, formal verification, and semantics-preserving code generation into a traceable workflow. It is implemented in the LoongMeta toolchain and evaluated using representative functions from the Hualong One (HPR1000) reactor protection system and the Linglong One (ACP100) power control system. The evaluation achieved an automatic code generation rate of 90%, 100% behavioral consistency between the design models and generated C code, and an approximately 30% improvement in overall engineering efficiency. Overall, these results show that the deep integration of model-driven development and formal methods provides a practical, traceable, and quantitatively assessable approach to quality assurance for safety-critical nuclear I&C software.

title: The fission matrix method for criticality search in Heat-Pipe Micro Reactors
abstract: In this work the Fission Matrix (FM) method is proposed to conduct the neutronics analysis of a Heat-Pipe Micro Reactor (HPMR). The aim of this model is to support the real-time modelling of heat-pipe-based microreactor designs, which have recently gained significant industrial interest. A database of FMs is generated through different criticality calculations, each of them considering a different core configuration (temperature profile and control drums position). The database is then interpolated to generate, in principle, the results for any arbitrary core layout. In this study the accuracy decrease of the FM method in the presence of a temperature difference between the core and the reflector is highlighted and addressed. The accuracy of the method is assessed through comparison with reference Serpent 2 simulations. Different core temperature profiles and control drum positions are tested. Finally, leveraging the computational efficiency and high accuracy of the FM, a criticality search algorithm is developed. Overall, the results show very good agreement with the corresponding Serpent 2 reference cases, while requiring only a very short computational time.

title: Design, dynamic analysis, and optimization of a hybrid nuclear-storage power system for mobile applications
abstract: With the rapid advancement of heat pipe-cooled reactor (HPR) technology, the integration of mobile nuclear power with energy storage offers a promising solution for energy supply in remote and off-grid scenarios. However, existing research predominantly focuses on stationary systems, lacking comprehensive investigation into the dynamic coupling of HPRs and hybrid storage in mobile environments. To address this gap, this paper proposes a novel hybrid nuclear-storage power system (HNSPS) integrating an HPR with a lithium-ion battery and supercapacitor for mobile applications. A high-fidelity system model is developed in MATLAB/Simulink, incorporating a nuclear power generation system, hybrid energy storage, and control models. A fully active parallel topology is employed for the storage subsystem, utilizing lithium-ion batteries for baseload and supercapacitors for transient power fluctuation mitigation. Simulation results demonstrate robust synergistic operation, characterized by excellent dynamic response and energy management performance. Parameter optimization indicates that the lithium battery rated voltage (determined by series configuration) should balance cycle life and manufacturing cost, while its response time should be extended for high-frequency operation and shortened for high-power-demand scenarios. For the supercapacitor, an initial voltage of 100–200 V and a series number of approximately 200 are recommended to balance transient power capability, safety, and cost. This work validates the feasibility and reliability of the proposed HNSPS for mobile scenarios, providing a theoretical reference for the deployment of mobile nuclear energy applications.

title: Expanding the capabilities of physics-informed neural networks through parametrisation for the neutron diffusion equation
abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have emerged as a promising alternative for solving systems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs), such as the neutron diffusion equation. Here, conventional PINNs assume fixed PDE parameters, however, in reality, the material parameters inside a nuclear reactor core vary continuously. The variation renders the conventional fixed parameters PINNs unsuitable as the models must be retrained. To address this challenge, a parametric PINNs model is built so inferences can be made on various material properties without the need for retraining. This article aims to demonstrates the capabilities of PINNs in resolving the neutron diffusion equation with fixed parameters in both one-dimensional and two-dimensional geometries and compared to the reference finite difference solver. Then, the functionality of PINNs is extended by training the network across a range of material parameters pertaining to real physical changes in reactor conditions generated through OpenMC. The model is then verified against a reference solver on one-hundred random material properties within the OpenMC generated range, showing good agreement with the reference solution but with a vastly accelerated calculation routine.

title: Mobile Low-Dwell Time Robotic Radiation Mapping Using Auto-Regressive Multi-Fidelity Gaussian Processes (ARGP) in Saturated Radiological Environments
abstract: This work presents an evaluation of a multi-fidelity Gaussian Process (GP) framework for fusing sparse, high-accuracy “ground-truth” radiation measurements with the dense, lower-accuracy data stream of a mobile robotic platform into a single, continuous dose-rate map with quantified uncertainty. The framework is structured in two stages: (i) an offline kernel-selection stage that fits an additive log-space discrepancy model against a fixed-location site control survey, and (ii) an online deployment stage that re-uses the offline low-fidelity GP as a Kennedy and O’Hagan auto-regressive prior over a fresh GP fit on the live robot stream. Survey data collected at a university research reactor drives the evaluation, where cross-validation across four candidate covariance kernels (Radial Basis Function, Matérn 3/2, Matérn 5/2, and Rational Quadratic) is used to assess predictive accuracy and uncertainty calibration against the control. Three results follow from treating the validation itself as an object of study. A paired bootstrap over the 21 control points shows the four kernels to be all but indistinguishable under leave-one-out cross-validation, with 34 of 36 paired differences in root mean square error containing zero. A ranking emerges only under repeated spatially-blocked cross-validation, where both Matérn kernels beat the alternatives on every trial and the ordering is close to the reverse of the leave-one-out one, quantifying how much spatial leakage that protocol admits. The model’s systematic under-prediction of high-dose zones, between 19% and 58% depending on trial and blocking radius, is shown to be substantially a property of the constant-variance likelihood rather than of data sparsity alone: substituting the detector’s Poisson counting variance removes the bias on one trial and reduces it on the others, at a cost in overall error. The selected kernel is then deployed on the robot during near real-time mapping, where the model produces continuous heatmaps of the predicted dose rate and its paired uncertainty, supporting situational awareness and conservative dose-bound planning. The primary contribution is a quantitative characterization of how the combined framework behaves on a real reactor cell, including which of its assumptions are load-bearing and which are not, and how its uncertainty output can guide conservative dose planning and active sampling.

title: Monte Carlo simulations to determine counting efficiencies in whole-body counting measurement considering age, gender, and radionuclide biokinetics
abstract: A large radiological release can result in internal contamination of the affected population, necessitating assessment through population monitoring methods such as whole-body counting measurements. Accurate calibration of whole-body counting systems is essential for reliable contamination assessment. However, conventional calibration methods using physical phantoms do not account for age- or gender-dependent anatomical variability. Moreover, inhaled or ingested radionuclides present radionuclide-specific biokinetics, resulting in heterogeneous activity distributions within the body that can substantially affect counting efficiency. To address these limitations, this study aims to determine time-dependent counting efficiencies for whole-body counting measurement using Monte Carlo-based calibration methods with age- and gender-specific computational human phantoms. Biodistribution data for radionuclides, including 137 Cs, 134 Cs, and 131 I, following intake are applied to the phantoms to estimate counting efficiencies. The results demonstrate that counting efficiencies are influenced by age- and gender-related anatomical differences and vary with post-intake time because of changes in biodistribution. This effect is particularly pronounced for 131 I, for which heterogeneous distribution results in significant variations in counting efficiency. By incorporating both biokinetic behavior and anatomical characteristics, the proposed approach provides more realistic estimates of counting efficiency than conventional calibration methods, thereby reducing systematic errors and supporting more accurate internal contamination assessments during radiological emergencies.

title: Impact of load conditions on single event transients in power supply circuit
abstract: Single-event transients (SETs) of the power supply circuit are investigated by conducting heavy-ion tests. The most sensitive device in the circuit whose SET response dominates the circuit functional degradation is identified. Then the impact of load currents and load types on the SET cross section of the sensitive device is analyzed. A combination of circuit characteristics tests and SPICE simulations is used to illustrate the mechanism of the influence on device SETs response under different load conditions. The research results may provide valuable assistance for power supply circuit design and device application.

title: An Efficient Prediction Method of Effective Shunt Impedance for IH-Type Drift Tube Linacs
abstract: : In conventional drift tube linac (DTL) design, the determination of radio-frequency (RF) parameters relies heavily on iterative three-dimensional (3D) electromagnetic (EM) simulations, which imposes several limitations, including low efficiency in evaluating multiple design schemes. To overcome this challenge, an efficient RF parameters prediction method for IH-type DTL cavities based on the Single-Cell Database Prediction (SCDP) is proposed in this paper. Multi-cell cavity models are constructed from optimized single-cell models to determine correction factors that account for the effects of undercuts and half-drift tube sections. By combining the single-cell database with beam dynamics parameters, SCDP method can efficiently predict the RF parameters of the entire cavity. Numerical validation based on the DTL1 cavity of the Ultra-rapid Cycling Accelerator Facility (UCAF) shows that the effective shunt impedance predicted by this method differs from the CST simulation result of the full-cavity model within 2%, demonstrating the numerical feasibility of the proposed method for the investigated cavity.

title: Activation of the dosimetric properties of potassium chloride crystal via doping with lithium ions
abstract: A high-temperature thermally stimulated luminescence (TSL) peak at 505 K has been identified in KCl:Li crystals. Its integral light yield ( η KCl:Li ) increases linearly with lithium ion concentration ( η KCl:Li ∼ f(С Li )), and with the dose of X-ray and gamma irradiation ( η KCl:Li ∼ f(D )). Moreover, it substantially exceeds the light yield of the dosimetric TSL peak at 495 K in the widely used TLD-100 (LiF:Mg,Ti) ( η KCl:Li >> η LiF:Mg,Ti ). The enhancement of the integral TSL light yield ( η KCl:Li ) at 505 K is attributed to an increase in the concentration of hole-type V 2 , V 3, V 4A -centers and electron-type F , F A (Li)-centers, as established by absorption, thermally activated, and luminescence spectroscopy. In KCl crystal lattice lithium ions act as catalysts of the efficient formation of both halogen centers (predominantly V 3 -centers with an absorption band peaking at 5.8 eV) and electron F -centers (2.3 eV). Upon their thermal dissociation, they serve as luminescence centers by facilitating the sequential recombination of electrons and holes released from ionized defect states.

title: Study on four-quadrant performance testing and numerical simulation of a reactor coolant pump model
abstract: This study presents an integrated experimental–numerical investigation of the four-quadrant performance of a scaled reactor coolant pump (RCP) model. Four-quadrant experiments were conducted on a high-precision test rig to obtain the pump head, torque, and flow rate under different quadrant operating conditions. The experimental data were subsequently normalized to generate dimensionless homologous characteristic curves. Due to the limitations of the experimental setup under extreme operating conditions, numerical simulations were performed to supplement the data near the zero-flow point and under very high flow rate conditions. By combining the experimental and numerical results, a smooth and continuous full-range pump characteristic curve was obtained, which can be used in transient thermal–hydraulic analyses of reactor systems. The results improve the understanding of RCP behavior under off-design and reverse operating conditions and provide support for the development of reliable pump models for nuclear safety analyses.

title: Full-core design of helical cruciform fuel for power uprate in water-cooled SMRs
abstract: Helical cruciform fuel (HCF) has been proposed as an advanced fuel design for water-cooled reactors, offering enhanced safety margins through an increased heat transfer area and the potential for higher core power density compared with standard cylindrical fuel. However, comprehensive full-core neutronics design studies of HCF remain limited, particularly those exploring power uprates across different fuel forms. The unique helical geometry presents challenges for traditional two-step lattice homogenization approaches, motivating the use of direct three-dimensional full-core simulation. In this work, continuous-energy Monte Carlo simulations using the Serpent code are employed to perform a design study of three core configurations: a UO 2 cylindrical fuel core, a U-50Zr HCF core, and a UO 2 HCF core. The core design methodology is established and then applied to design U-50Zr and UO 2 HCF cores with consistent core dimensions and operating conditions. A comprehensive comparison is performed across all three configurations, evaluating key design parameters for the equilibrium cycle, such as core reactivity, critical boron letdown, power peaking factors, and reactivity coefficients. The cost assessment demonstrates that the HCF-enabled uprated core design is economically competitive with the reference design. Detailed transient safety assessments and further validation of the underlying cost assumptions remain subjects for future investigation. This study provides the first direct three-dimensional Monte Carlo core design of a water-cooled small modular reactor employing HCF for power uprate, integrated with fuel performance and economic assessments.

title: Applications of artificial intelligence technology in space nuclear reactor systems
abstract: Space nuclear power systems have attracted increasing attention as enabling technologies for future deep-space exploration because of their high energy density, long-duration power generation capability, and independence from terrestrial environmental conditions. Artificial intelligence (AI) has shown considerable potential for addressing key challenges in space nuclear systems, including intelligent design optimization, state prediction, fault diagnosis, and autonomous operation. This review provides a systematic overview of AI applications in space nuclear power systems, with particular emphasis on current capabilities, limitations, and future development directions. The classifications, system architectures, and representative technologies of space nuclear reactors are first introduced to establish the engineering context and identify the challenges that motivate AI integration. Machine learning (ML), intelligent optimization algorithm (IOA), deep learning (DL), reduced-order model (ROM), and data assimilation (DA) are reviewed with emphasis on their applicability under the specific constraints of space nuclear systems, including limited sensing capability, stringent size, weight, and power (SWaP) requirements, radiation environments, and scarce operational data. Representative AI applications are discussed in terms of system design optimization, state prediction and digital twins (DTs), fault diagnosis, health management, and prospective autonomous operation. The current maturity of AI-enabled applications in space nuclear systems is also assessed. Existing studies rely primarily on high-fidelity simulations, ground-based demonstrations, and transferable methodologies from terrestrial nuclear engineering, while operational data from space nuclear reactors remain unavailable. Key challenges associated with onboard computational limitations, radiation-induced hardware degradation, model reliability, and verification and validation (V&V) requirements are also discussed. Future research directions toward trustworthy AI, physics-informed learning, adaptive digital twins, and intelligent autonomous operation frameworks are then summarized. This review provides a reference for understanding the current status and future potential of AI technologies in space nuclear power systems.

title: Taxonomies of levels of automation for small modular reactors based on operational conditions
abstract: Many fields, including the nuclear energy industry, commonly use a taxonomy of levels of automation (LOAs) as a reference for function allocation, a process conducted to determine whether functions are assigned to humans or automation. An emerging issue is that existing LOA taxonomies have limitations when applied to small modular reactors (SMRs), as SMRs tend to adopt higher levels of automation and expanded passive safety systems than large nuclear power plants. This paper proposes detailed LOA taxonomies that reflect the operational characteristics of SMRs under different operational conditions—normal, abnormal, and emergency conditions—with specific consideration of operator support systems as a major automation domain. For normal operations, the LOA taxonomies are divided into system automation and operation automation based on whether control systems are utilized. For abnormal operations, in which operators’ cognitive functions are emphasized, the taxonomy is classified based on data acquisition, diagnosis, and abnormal operating procedure implementation, with various roles of automation as an operator support system. For emergency conditions, the taxonomy integrates the concepts of passive safety systems and automation. The proposed LOA taxonomies provide a foundation for defining human–automation roles in greater detail from the early stage of SMR design, as well as support designers in considering different types and levels of operator support systems.

title: Numerical investigation of top-flooding debris bed quenching FLOAT experiments
abstract: Safety relevant questions during severe accidents in a nuclear power plant may concern the ex-vessel debris bed coolability in combination with molten corium concrete interaction. The behaviour within the debris bed is expected to be multidimensional, as the bed may be irregular in geometry, composed of heterogeneous particles, exhibit spatially varying porosity, be flooded from different directions, partially re-melt due to local or global dry out, and be affected by non-condensable gases. Fundamental investigation of such conditions requires consideration of multidimensional behaviour. It can be supported by top-flooding experiments and simulations with validated computer codes. This paper evaluates the suitability of an axisymmetric description for analysing multidimensional behaviour during debris bed quenching under top-flooding conditions. Analyses of recent FLOAT experiments (IKE, Germany) show that the multidimensionality of the quenching process is governed by the location of the penetrating water. A detailed numerical investigation performed with the MC3D code (ASNR, France) provides additional valuable insights supporting the interpretation of the experimental results. The axisymmetric modelling shows good qualitative agreement with the measurements. An improved quantitative description is possible with non-axisymmetric modelling. Sensitivity to air flow, initial temperature, porosity, and friction modelling is observed.

title: Joint study on anomaly detection and remaining useful life prediction of ex-core neutron detector in nuclear power plant under interference factors
abstract: The remaining useful life (RUL) prediction of the ex-core neutron detector is needed to provide helpful references for reactor operation, enable equipment condition monitoring, and enhance condition-based maintenance (CBM) in nuclear power plant (NPP). Most equipment RUL prediction systems fail to integrate anomaly detection methods to determine the onset time of anomalies and neglect the interference factors generating the outliers. We demonstrate the effectiveness of combining the virtual redundancy anomaly detection model with the RUL prediction model in overcoming these issues, based on operational data from a set of real-world intermediate range detectors (IRDs). We also propose an outlier detection method to remove the outliers generated by interference factors. Moreover, a RUL prediction model and a deterioration trend tracking prediction model have been developed.

title: A new stochastic implicit depletion scheme with combined nuclide-flux relaxation and a review of computational efficiency and accuracy for stochastic implicit depletion schemes
abstract: Depletion calculations using the Monte-Carlo method for neutron transport commonly suffer from numerical instabilities due to a phenomenon known as xenon-power oscillations. Such oscillations are physical in nature and are regularly observed in real nuclear reactors; but the feedback between spatial xenon concentration and the spatial power distribution in most Monte-Carlo depletion simulations is nonphysical and creates stability issues when depletion is modeled in optically thick problems such as full-length fuel assemblies or full cores. The equilibrium xenon approach or stochastic implicit (SI) depletion schemes are commonly used to ameliorate these issues as resolving xenon-power oscillations by simply increasing the number of simulated histories is usually an intractable approach. This study extends a previously proposed constant relaxation predictor–corrector SI approach (SI-CE/LI) by considering a new scheme with constant relaxation of both the spatial nuclide density and flux (or power) distributions. The new scheme is called the SI-CE/LI-Flux-Nuclide (SI-CE/LI-FN) scheme. Combined relaxation of both the spatial nuclide and flux distributions has a synergistic effect and the proposed methodology is able to obtain stable solutions to a 700 cm tall Fluoride-salt High temperature Reactor fuel assembly problem. With properly chosen relaxation factors, performance is equal, or better, than that of single-field relaxation approaches used in SI depletion schemes. Moreover, SI approaches offer a new way to split computational effort in already computationally intense depletion calculations; therefore, the apportioning of computational effort when using SI schemes is further investigated and practical guidance is given for users of SI depletion schemes.

title: Source-term modeling of radioactive krypton and xenon in activated carbon delay beds for molten salt reactor off-gas systems
abstract: Radioactive krypton (Kr) and xenon (Xe) continuously released from liquid-fueled molten salt reactors are transported to the cover-gas and off-gas treatment systems, where activated carbon delay beds play an important role in source-term control. This study develops a transient modeling framework for Kr/Xe transport, retention, decay, and activity evolution in activated carbon delay beds. The one-dimensional model couples axial convection, axial dispersion, linear driving force adsorption, Henry-equilibrium adsorption, and radioactive decay. The formulation is extended to multi-nuclide decay chains, allowing gaseous daughters to continue transport and adsorption while treating non-gaseous daughters as locally deposited products. Reactor-condition-dependent inlet source terms are provided through one-way coupling with MACT-based multi-node source-term calculations, including upstream holdup and pre-bed decay. The numerical implementation is verified against an analytical solution under the local-equilibrium limit and using the Method of Manufactured Solutions (MMS) for finite-rate Henry–LDF coupling, while the adsorption model is evaluated against dilute Kr fixed-bed breakthrough data. A reference case inspired by the Molten Salt Reactor Experiment (MSRE) is then analyzed to examine isotope-dependent penetration, parent-decay feeding, phase-resolved activity distribution, nuclide-wise activity contributions, and shutdown residual activity. The results show strong isotope-dependent attenuation: Kr-85m falls below 10 −3 of its inlet concentration at x/L ≈ 0.224, whereas Kr-85 penetrates the full bed and Xe-131m remains measurable at the outlet. Parent decay can noticeably enhance daughter concentrations; for the Kr-85m→Kr-85 chain, in-bed feeding increases the maximum normalized Kr-85 concentration to approximately 2.3. At 180 d, the adsorbed and deposited inventories account for approximately 99.6% of the bed-integrated activity, while the gas phase accounts for only 0.38%. Following shutdown, continued helium purge reduces the gas-phase inventory to 10.8% of its shutdown value at 0.83 d, whereas the total residual activity decreases more slowly, reaching 0.7% of its shutdown value at 30 d.

title: Research on water radiolysis models and their behavior in high flux research reactors
abstract: A water radiolysis model is developed for high flux research reactors, with application to the Tsinghua High Flux Reactor (THFR). Refined G-value calculations (gamma and neutron) and supplemented reactions for alkaline conditions are validated against literature experiments, showing good agreement. Parametric studies reveal that molecular product concentrations scale with the square root of the dose rate due to the bimolecular nature of elementary reactions, and decrease with temperature, with a progressively slowing rate of decrease, reflecting different temperature dependencies of the competing production and consumption kinetics. THFR simulations show steady state reached within ∼1 s in most regions. Notably, despite the dose rate being two orders of magnitude lower than that in the core, upper and lower plena exhibit significant importance on the coolant radiolysis due to the square root scaling and long residence times.
